items: Know Your Contract Before Signing, Item 1: Request the complete 40-60 page contract from any warranty company before you sign and read every section on exclusions and definitions to understand exactly what could be used against you later.

Know Your Contract Before Signing, Item 2: Compare the company's coverage caps against actual replacement costs from sources like HomeAdvisor to understand the real financial gap between what they pay and what the repair actually costs.

Know Your Contract Before Signing, Item 3: Identify every vague or undefined term in the contract such as normal wear and tear or improper installation that the company could apply after the fact to justify a denial.

Know Your Contract Before Signing, Item 4: Keep dated receipts and service records from licensed HVAC and appliance technicians to prove maintenance was performed on schedule, because most contracts require documented proof of service.

Protect Yourself During Claims, Item 1: Document all communications with the warranty company including dates, names, email addresses, and exact quotes from every conversation to build a verifiable record of what was said.

Protect Yourself During Claims, Item 2: Get an independent assessment from a licensed technician before accepting any denial to understand whether the denial has merit and what the actual repair should cost.

Protect Yourself During Claims, Item 3: Request the technician's full written report from the warranty company's vendor network before the coverage decision is made so you can identify errors or omissions.

Protect Yourself During Claims, Item 4: Ask the warranty company to explain the specific contract clause justifying each denial point and document their response, because vague denials without specific citations are easier to appeal.

Fight Back After a Denial, Item 1: File a formal written appeal that directly cites the contract language and specific facts that contradict the denial reasoning, and send it via certified mail with return receipt requested.
Fight Back After a Denial, Item 2: Submit a complaint to your state insurance commissioner or consumer protection office to create an official record of the denial and trigger regulatory scrutiny.

Fight Back After a Denial, Item 3: Report the company to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau if they violate federal disclosure or claims handling requirements, which can trigger federal investigation.

Fight Back After a Denial, Item 4: Consult a consumer rights attorney if the denial appears to follow a pattern of bad faith conduct rather than legitimate coverage disputes, because class action lawsuits have successfully recovered damages for systematic denials.
